Hiring Alert: Senior Full Stack Engineer (TypeScript / NestJS / React / AWS)
We are looking for a Senior Full Stack Engineer to join the team at Valerie! You will play a pivotal role in developing and operating our multi-tenant platform, which powers brand onboarding, market analysis, forecasting, business valuation, document generation, and cutting-edge AI-enabled workflows.
If you are a hands-on engineer who loves owning features from frontend design all the way to production monitoring and infrastructure, we want to hear from you!

💡 What You Will Do
End-to-End Ownership: Design and ship production features across React, NestJS, and PostgreSQL, maintaining shared TypeScript and Zod contracts.
Complex UI & Architecture: Build sophisticated, schema-driven forms with validation, autosave, conditional sections, rich text editing, and role-based behaviors.
AI-Enabled Workflows: Integrate LLM/model APIs, structured outputs, tool use, retrieval, webhooks, and asynchronous processing into our platform.
Robust Backend & Data Layer: Develop well-structured REST APIs and design relational schemas, migrations, and transactions in PostgreSQL with secure authentication/authorization.
Infrastructure & DevSecOps: Manage production infrastructure on AWS (ECS/EC2, ALB, RDS, S3) using Terraform (IaC), Docker, and automated CI/CD pipelines.
Quality & Reliability: Write comprehensive unit, integration, and E2E tests (Jest, Playwright) while ensuring high system observability.

🎯 What We're Looking For
Experience: 5–8 years of relevant production engineering experience with substantial system ownership.
TypeScript Expertise: 3+ years of advanced TypeScript development (generics, discriminated unions, strict mode, utility types) across frontend and backend.
Frontend Mastery: Advanced React experience (component architecture, server state, hooks) and schema validation libraries (Zod, React Hook Form).
Backend & API Skills: Strong Node.js and NestJS experience alongside practical REST API design (idempotency, pagination, versioning).
Database & Cloud: Solid PostgreSQL skills (indexing, constraints, migrations) and hands-on AWS production experience paired with Terraform.
AI Integration: Real-world experience shipping production AI-enabled workflows involving LLMs (no personal experimentation-only backgrounds).

🌟 Our Company Values
We live and breathe our core values in our day-to-day operations:
Accountability: Own your part in it first.
Collaboration: Take initiative with discipline and humility.
Resilience: Be steadfast, assess, and bounce back.
Selflessness: Focus on what it takes to scale together.
Fun: Be present and connect.

The hardest part of directing a research lab isn't the science.
It’s managing everything around it.

I direct the Psoriatic Arthritis and Spondyloarthritis Center at Vanderbilt.

Our program runs on 5 people:
↳ My clinical partner who recruits from their clinic
↳ A research coordinator: recruitment, REDCap, IRB
↳ A research trainee: chart abstraction
↳ A research assistant: charts, abstracts, papers
↳ Me

My job is making sure none of them is stuck.

7 lessons from directing my research lab:

1️⃣ Hiring is the biggest research decision I make
↳ If at all possible, hire on contract first. A small test project together beats any interview.

2️⃣ A slow decision costs > a wrong one
↳ A wrong coding rule costs one re-review. No rule means two abstractors coding the same chart two ways.

3️⃣ The leader sets the standards
↳ It starts with me. Late feedback from me makes deadlines optional. Aim to be relentlessly reliable.

4️⃣ Missed work is a skill problem or a motivation problem
↳ Skill: a worked example fixes it.
↳ Motivation: training won't. A different task or a bigger challenge often will.

5️⃣ The person closest to the data knows things I don't
↳ I ask my abstractor: are my clinic notes leaving any variable missing systematically?

6️⃣ People do better work when they buy the WHY
↳ An abstractor who knows the research question flags the odd case.
↳ A team that buys into the mission makes small decisions without me.

7️⃣ People are the most important asset of any lab.
↳ Protect: before any "quick data pull," I ask whose hours it takes.
↳ Nurture: help them get where they want to go. Even out of my lab.

Doer to leader is the hardest promotion in research.

It's also the one nobody prepares you for.

Mastering backend API testing concepts is essential for QA Engineers and SDETs. Here is a breakdown of key technical domains frequently covered in API interviews:

🔹 𝟭. 𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗙𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 & 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴
• Core Mechanics: API validation, request/response headers, status codes, and JSON/XML payloads.
• Protocol Types: Web APIs (REST/GraphQL/gRPC), OS APIs, Library APIs.
• Testing Tools: Postman, Bruno, SoapUI, Swagger/OpenAPI.

🔹 𝟮. 𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝘃𝘀. 𝗦𝗢𝗔𝗣 𝗔𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲
• REST: Architectural style using JSON/XML, stateless, highly scalable.
• SOAP: Strict XML-based protocol with built-in enterprise security (WS-Security).

🔹 𝟯. 𝗛𝗧𝗧𝗣 𝗠𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗱𝘀 & 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝘂𝘀 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲𝘀
• HTTP Verbs: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE.
• Status Ranges: 2xx (Success), 3xx (Redirection), 4xx (Client Errors), 5xx (Server Errors).

🔹 𝟰. 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 & 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
• Auth Mechanisms: Basic Auth, Bearer Tokens, OAuth 2.0, API Keys, JWT.
• Security Risks: Input validation, rate limiting, CORS, OWASP API Top 10 vulnerabilities.

🔹 𝟱. 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 & 𝗖𝗜/𝗖𝗗
• Advanced Approaches: API mocking, service virtualization, contract testing (Pact).
• Pipeline Integration: Automated REST API execution in CI/CD pipelines.

There is a worker in your company nobody hired. No one graded it, no one noticed, and HR pays its salary as a software licence.
Every other function that took on the same kind of worker this year did not make that mistake.
SAP put a connected network of AI agents into SuccessFactors this year, across recruiting, performance, and talent development. In hiring, the agents screen the applicants, draft the job post, schedule the interviews and message the candidate. In talent, an agent reads one employee's skills against a target role, checks them against the skills taxonomy and the market, and writes the development path to close the gap. A form does not do that. That is the judgement a talent partner used to hold, now carried out by something HR pays for as a licence and never put on a payroll.
Finance and operations got the same class of agent and treated it as an arrival, not a purchase. They asked what it decides without a human, who checks it, who signs for what it produces. They grade it, because a wrong number will not balance and a stopped line is visible from the yard. The error shows itself, so they had to look. HR's errors stay hidden. A weak shortlist looks like a normal shortlist. A bad development path reads as a reasonable plan. So HR kept reading the licence and missed that it had taken on staff.
Here is the objection, and it is fair. An agent is not a person. It has no employment relationship, no rights, no accountability of its own. Calling it a hire is a category error, and the whole thing is IT's problem anyway.
Half of that is correct. The agent has no contract and never will, and the accountability stays with the humans who switch it on. But the decisions it forces do not care what you call it. Something now sits between a candidate and a job, and between an employee and a promotion, and makes part of the call. What it is allowed to decide alone, who supervises that, who signs the outcome, how far it is trusted before a human has to step in. Those are grading and supervision decisions. They are HR's, not IT's. Refusing to treat the agent as staff does not remove them. It means nobody makes them, and the agent keeps deciding while the chart pretends it is not there.
So pick one, because there is no third box. Either the agent in your HR system is a hire you have not managed, or it is a tool that keeps making calls no tool should make alone. Both are yours to own. HR has admitted to neither.

Look, let’s cut through the Silicon Valley spin.

For the last few years, the tech sector ran on a simple mantra: move fast, break things, and let the lawyers clean up the mess later. 

Companies bolted AI onto everything from customer service to contract generation without asking the one question that actually matters on a balance sheet: Who owns the wreck when this thing goes off the road?

Now we’re finding out.

The honeymoon phase of unaccountable automation is crashing headfirst into actual legal liability. Courts and regulators aren't buying the old excuses anymore. If an autonomous model hallucinates a liability, scrapes IP it shouldn't have touched, or bakes bias into a hiring algorithm, the board can't just point at the software vendor and shrug.

In my corporate days running global sales teams, I learned one absolute truth: Velocity without intention is just a fast way to crash.

Corporate accountability in the age of disruption comes down to three non-negotiables:

1. Passive oversight is zero oversight. Having a human casually glance at an AI output doesn't cut it in a courtroom or a boardroom. If you can't audit the decision path, you don't own the process—you're just gambling.

2. Vendor risk is your balance sheet. Too many companies sign enterprise AI contracts without looking at who carries the liability when the model goes rogue. 

3. If your supplier's hallucination triggers a lawsuit, your name is on the complaint.
 
The Wild West is closed. 

Regulatory guardrails aren't an IT checkbox anymore; they are part of the core operating model.

We don't need more tech utopias. We need operators who understand that real strategy means building the guardrails before you hit the gas.

Last week was… a lot.
Health issues, almost 3 hours of waiting at the border, and a 15-hour journey from Niš to Portorož. And all of that to be a speaker at NT Conference.

Was it worth it? Absolutely.
It was such an incredible experience to share the panel with Tomaz Valjavec, Maša Košak, Gorazd Justinek, and Nataša Briški and discuss a topic that is becoming more relevant every day: how AI will influence people development and how the hiring process is already changing. I shared one very concrete example from Codekido.
We recently opened a position for a Junior DevOps Engineer and received 157 CVs.
And you can clearly see the impact of AI. CVs are becoming more polished, more structured, and often very similar to one another. It raises an interesting question:

Where is the boundary between using AI as a tool and letting an AI agent completely represent you?

AI can help us write better, prepare faster, and present our experience more clearly. But I still believe something personal needs to remain in the process: your way of thinking, your motivation, your story, and the things that make you different from the other 156 applicants.

After the conference, I spent the rest of the week talking to people across Slovenia. I met engineers who inspired me to do more, build more, and think bigger. But I also learned something equally important from the business side. I met people who showed genuine care for a potential client before there was even a signed contract. They asked questions. They tried to understand the problem. They invested their time. They cared about whether the solution would actually work - without knowing whether there would be a commercial relationship at the end.

That left a strong impression on me.
Because in our industry, it is very easy to start caring about a client after the contract is signed. The companies and people who stand out are often the ones who care before it is signed. That is something I want us to continue building into Codekido's culture as well. Thanks a lot, Katarina Adamovic and Anica Vrekic, for being with me on this trip. 

And finally, a huge thank you to Inženjerka godine Srbija and Edita Krajnovic for allowing me to represent Codekido in Slovenia. 

Despite the exhausting start to the week, I came home with more energy, ideas, and motivation than I left with. Sometimes the most difficult journeys really are worth making.

Connecticut's new AI employment law goes live in a few days, and it brings a harsh reality check that most employers haven't absorbed yet: your vendor contract doesn't cover you.

Taking effect October 1, the law places the compliance burden squarely on the deployer — i.e., the employer using the AI system — not the third-party developer that built it. A standard software license agreement does not move that legal obligation.

Here is what employers need to track:
➤ What's covered: AI used in hiring, promotion, discipline, and termination — resume screeners, performance management tools, workforce analytics, and automated ranking systems. Most HR teams will be surprised by how much is already baked into their workflows.
➤ What's required: Risk management frameworks, impact assessments, transparency notices, and mechanisms for human review/appeal where feasible.
➤ What's enforceable: Violations trigger unfair trade practice penalties (up to $5,000 per violation via the Attorney General). While there's no private right of action, using AI is explicitly barred as a defense against discrimination claims, leaving existing federal and state anti-discrimination exposure fully intact.

The practical takeaway is a procurement one.

If your vendor agreements don't explicitly obligate providers to supply bias-audit results, technical documentation, and active cooperation with impact assessments, you are carrying compliance exposure your contracts never accounted for. Review your vendor contracts before you audit your models.

Connecticut is setting the precedent on deployer-side accountability, but it won't be the last. Employers building an inventory of their AI tools and tightening vendor-management discipline today will have the exact playbook ready when the next state follows.

How is your organization handling AI vendor risk? Are your contracts ready for what's coming?

I used Postman for 18 months. Thought I was doing API testing. Then a senior interviewer asked me one question. I had no answer.
 
"How do you validate that your API hasn't broken its contract with 3 downstream consumers?"
 
I said: "I'd check the response in Postman."
 
He nodded. Interview ended shortly after.
 
That failure taught me what API testing actually means at a senior level.

What juniors answer:

Send request → check status code → check response body

What seniors answer:

Contract validation across consumers
Schema drift detection
State injection to remove UI dependency
Mocking downstream failures to test resilience
Performance degradation thresholds, not just pass or fail
 
The difference isn't tools. It's the questions you know to ask before writing a single test.
 
Postman is where API exploration begins. Not where API testing ends.
 
It's the mindset shift most SDETs take years to make.
 
What was your "I didn't know what I didn't know" API testing moment?

I used Postman for 18 months. Thought I was doing API testing. Then a senior interviewer asked me one question. I had no answer.
 
"How do you validate that your API hasn't broken its contract with 3 downstream consumers?"
 
I said: "I'd check the response in Postman."
 
He nodded. Interview ended shortly after.
 
That failure taught me what API testing actually means at a senior level.

What juniors answer:

Send request → check status code → check response body

What seniors answer:

Contract validation across consumers
Schema drift detection
State injection to remove UI dependency
Mocking downstream failures to test resilience
Performance degradation thresholds, not just pass or fail
 
The difference isn't tools. It's the questions you know to ask before writing a single test.
 
Postman is where API exploration begins. Not where API testing ends.
 
It's the mindset shift most SDETs take years to make.
 
What was your "I didn't know what I didn't know" API testing moment?
